tips.title: Two rays, always the same two
tips.body: **Parallel to the axis, then through F**; and **straight through the centre**, undeviated. Where they cross is the image. Every lens ray diagram is built from those two, so there is nothing to choose.

tips.title: Far side means inverted
tips.body: An image where the rays **actually cross** is **real and inverted**; one on the **same side** as the object is **virtual and upright**. If your diagram has an upright image on the far side, a ray is wrong — and the check takes two seconds.

tips.title: Magnification has no unit
tips.body: It is a length divided by a length. Write **3**, never *3 cm*. And convert first if the heights are in different units: 30 mm against 2 cm is a magnification of **1.5**, not 15.

tips.title: Arrowheads out for convex
tips.body: The symbol mirrors the effect: **outwards** for the lens that pulls rays **together**, **inwards** for the one that spreads them **apart**. Drawn that way you can never label the wrong lens.

tips.title: Dashed means the light is not there
tips.body: Lines traced **backwards** to a virtual image are drawn dashed, because no light travels along them. Drawing them solid claims light reaches a point it never does, and the mark scheme treats that as an error, not untidiness.

steps.title: What a lens does
steps.body:
**A lens forms an image by refracting light.** Light changes speed as it enters and leaves the glass, so it changes direction — and the curved shape of a lens is what makes all the rays bend by the right amount to meet.

There are two shapes, and they do opposite things.

**A convex lens** is **thicker in the middle**. It brings parallel rays **together**. Rays arriving parallel to the axis are brought to a focus at the **principal focus**, and

$$\textbf{the distance from the lens to the principal focus is the focal length.}$$

**A concave lens** is **thinner in the middle**. It makes parallel rays **spread apart**. They do not meet, but they appear to come from a principal focus on the **same side** the light came from.

A lens has a principal focus on **each** side, the same distance away, because light can pass through it either way.

A **fatter** lens — more strongly curved — bends light more, so its focal length is **shorter**.

steps.title: Drawing the ray diagram
steps.body:
A ray diagram is built from **construction rays** — rays whose path you already know. Two are enough to locate the image, and they are the same two every time.

**Ray 1.** From the top of the object, **parallel to the axis**, then refracted **through the principal focus** on the far side.

**Ray 2.** From the top of the object, **straight through the centre** of the lens, undeviated.

Where they cross is the top of the image.

steps.title: Real and virtual images
steps.body:
The distinction matters, and it is asked directly.

**A real image** is formed where light rays **actually meet**. Because the light is really there, a real image can be **projected onto a screen** — which is what a projector and the back of your eye both do. A real image formed by a single convex lens is always **inverted**.

**A virtual image** is formed where the rays only **appear** to come from. The light does not actually pass through that point, so a virtual image **cannot be projected onto a screen**. It is always **upright**.

The rules that follow:

- **A convex lens** forms a **real** image when the object is **beyond the focal length**, and a **virtual** image when the object is **closer than the focal length**. That second case is a **magnifying glass**: the image is upright, enlarged, and on the same side as the object.
- **A concave lens** always forms a **virtual** image, whatever the object distance — and it is always **upright** and **smaller** than the object.

On a ray diagram, the giveaway is which side the image is on. Rays crossing on the **far** side means a **real** image; rays that have to be traced **backwards**, drawn dashed, to a point on the **same** side means a **virtual** one.

steps.title: Magnification
steps.body:
**Magnification** compares the size of the image with the size of the object:

$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image height}}{\text{object height}}$$

Two things about it are examinable and easily lost:

- **Magnification is a ratio, so it has no units.** Writing *3 cm* for a magnification is wrong.
- The two heights must be measured in the **same unit** — both mm or both cm — or the ratio is meaningless.

A magnification **greater than 1** means the image is **larger** than the object; **less than 1** means **smaller**. A magnifying glass gives a magnification greater than 1; a camera photographing a building gives one far less than 1.

steps.title: Telling the two lenses apart in a diagram
steps.body:
Marks are given for the **symbols** as well as the rays, so the two must be drawn distinguishably.

- A **convex** lens is drawn as a vertical line with arrowheads pointing **outwards** at both ends.
- A **concave** lens is drawn as a vertical line with arrowheads pointing **inwards**.

The arrowheads mirror what the lens does to the light: outwards for the one that pulls rays **together**, inwards for the one that spreads them **apart**. That is worth knowing as a way of never drawing the wrong one.

**What each diagram must show:**

- the **principal axis**, drawn as a horizontal line
- the **lens symbol**, correct for the type
- **F** marked at the focal length on **both** sides
- the **object** as an arrow standing on the axis
- **at least two construction rays**, with the direction of travel
- the **image**, as an arrow — drawn **dashed** if it is virtual

The dashed lines matter. For a virtual image, the rays that reach the eye are real and solid; the lines traced **backwards** to where the image appears to be are **not** real light, so they are drawn dashed. Drawing them solid says the light is somewhere it is not.

steps.title: Going deeper: why a magnifying glass must be held close
steps.body:
**The rule and the reason.** A convex lens forms a **real** image when the object is **beyond** the focal length, and a **virtual, enlarged, upright** one when it is **inside** the focal length. A magnifying glass needs the second case — so the object must be **closer to the lens than the focal length**.

Why? Trace the rays. With the object inside F, the ray refracted at the lens is **still diverging** when it leaves: the lens has bent it, but not enough to make it converge. Diverging rays never meet, so no real image can form. Traced **backwards**, though, they appear to come from a point on the **same side** as the object, further away and **larger** — and that is what your eye sees.

This also explains what you notice using one: hold it too far from the page and the image **flips upside down** and shrinks. You have moved the object beyond the focal length and switched to the real-image case. The lens has not changed; the geometry has.

**Why a concave lens can never make a real image.** It **diverges** every ray. Rays that are spreading apart when they leave the lens can never cross, so they can never meet to form a real image. Whatever the object distance, the image can only be where the rays **appear** to come from — virtual, upright, and smaller.

**Being exact about dashed lines.** Dashed construction lines represent light that **is not there**. Drawing a virtual image's rays solid claims light passes through a point it never reaches — so it is not a presentational nicety but a statement about the physics, and the mark scheme treats it that way.

**Magnification traps.**

- It has **no units**. It is a length divided by a length.
- The heights must be in the **same unit**. An image 30 mm tall and an object 2 cm tall gives a magnification of 1.5, not 15.
- **Image over object**, not the other way round. Getting it inverted turns a magnification of 3 into 0.33, and the two describe opposite situations.

**A check on any ray diagram.** If your image came out on the far side of the lens, it should be **inverted**; if it came out on the same side, it should be **upright**. An image drawn on the far side but the same way up as the object has a construction error in it, and the check takes two seconds.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **A lens forms an image by refracting light.**
- A **convex** lens is **thicker in the middle** and brings parallel rays **together** at the **principal focus**.
- A **concave** lens is **thinner in the middle** and makes parallel rays **spread apart**.
- The **focal length** is the distance from the lens to the **principal focus**, and there is one on each side.
- **Two construction rays** locate the image: one **parallel to the axis then through F**, one **straight through the centre**.
- A **real** image forms where rays **actually meet**, can be **projected on a screen**, and from a single convex lens is **inverted**.
- A **virtual** image forms where rays only **appear** to come from, **cannot be projected**, and is **upright**.
- **Convex**: real when the object is **beyond** F; **virtual and enlarged** when it is **inside** F — the magnifying glass.
- **Concave**: **always virtual**, upright and smaller, whatever the object distance.
- $\text{magnification} = \dfrac{\text{image height}}{\text{object height}}$ — a **ratio, with no units**, and both heights in the **same unit**.
- Draw a **convex** lens with arrowheads pointing **out**, a **concave** lens with them pointing **in**.
- Lines traced **backwards** to a virtual image are **dashed**, because that light is not really there.

questions.prompt: Describe how to construct a ray diagram for a convex lens with the object placed beyond the focal length, and state the nature of the image formed.
questions.solution: First draw a horizontal line to represent the principal axis, and draw the lens as a vertical line crossing it with arrowheads pointing outwards at each end to show that it is convex. Mark the principal focus, F, on the axis at the focal length on both sides of the lens. Draw the object as an arrow standing upright on the axis, beyond the principal focus. Then draw the first construction ray from the top of the object travelling parallel to the principal axis until it reaches the lens, and from there refracting so that it passes through the principal focus on the far side and continues beyond it. Draw the second construction ray from the top of the object straight through the centre of the lens, where it carries on without being deviated. The point where these two rays cross is the top of the image, and the image is drawn as an arrow from that point to the principal axis. Because the rays actually cross, the image is real, and because it is formed below the axis it is inverted. It is formed on the opposite side of the lens from the object, and as it can be formed where light really is, it could be projected onto a screen.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Setting up.**

1. Draw the **principal axis** as a horizontal line.
2. Draw the lens as a vertical line across it, with **arrowheads pointing outwards** — the convex symbol.
3. Mark **F** at the focal length on **both** sides.
4. Draw the **object** as an upright arrow on the axis, **beyond F**.

**The two construction rays.**

- **Ray 1:** from the top of the object, **parallel to the axis** to the lens, then refracted **through F** on the far side and continuing beyond.
- **Ray 2:** from the top of the object **straight through the centre** of the lens, **undeviated**.

**The image.** Where the two rays **cross** is the top of the image; draw an arrow from there to the axis.

**Its nature.** The rays **actually cross**, so the image is **real**. It is below the axis, so it is **inverted**. It is on the **opposite side** from the object, and being real it **could be projected onto a screen**.

A check worth doing: an image on the far side must be inverted. If yours came out upright there, a ray has been drawn wrongly.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a real and a virtual image, and explain why a convex lens can form either while a concave lens can only ever form a virtual one.
questions.solution: A real image is formed at a point where light rays actually meet after passing through the lens. Because the light really is at that point, a real image can be projected onto a screen, and an image of this kind formed by a single convex lens is always inverted. A virtual image is formed at a point where the rays only appear to have come from, when they are traced backwards. No light actually passes through that point, so a virtual image cannot be projected onto a screen, and it is always upright. A convex lens can form either kind because it converges the rays. If the object is beyond the focal length the rays leaving the lens are converging and so they cross, producing a real image. If the object is closer to the lens than the focal length the rays leaving the lens are still diverging, so they never cross, and tracing them backwards gives an enlarged upright virtual image, which is how a magnifying glass works. A concave lens always diverges the light that passes through it, so the rays leaving it are always spreading apart and can never cross one another. Since a real image requires the rays to meet, a concave lens can never produce one, and the image can only ever be the virtual one seen by tracing the diverging rays backwards.

questions.modelAnswer:
**A real image** forms where light rays **actually meet** after the lens. The light really is there, so it **can be projected onto a screen**, and from a single convex lens it is always **inverted**.

**A virtual image** forms where the rays only **appear** to have come from, when traced backwards. No light passes through that point, so it **cannot be projected**, and it is always **upright**.

**Why a convex lens can form either.** It **converges** the rays:

- Object **beyond** the focal length → the rays leaving the lens are **converging**, so they **cross** → a **real** image.
- Object **inside** the focal length → the rays leaving are **still diverging**, so they never cross. Traced backwards they give an **enlarged, upright, virtual** image — the magnifying glass.

**Why a concave lens cannot.** It **always diverges** the light. Rays leaving it are always **spreading apart**, so they can **never cross**. A real image needs rays to meet, so a concave lens can only ever give the **virtual** image seen by tracing the diverging rays back.

The whole answer turns on one idea: a real image needs rays that **converge**, and only a convex lens can supply them.

examTechnique.body:
Draw the principal axis first, then the lens with the right arrowheads, then F on both sides.

Use the two standard construction rays and put arrows on them to show the direction of travel.

Say whether the image is real or virtual and upright or inverted, and draw it dashed if it is virtual.

For magnification, put the image height on top, check both heights are in the same unit, and give the answer with no unit.

When asked why a magnifying glass works, explain in terms of the object being inside the focal length and the rays still diverging.

Check the finished diagram: a far side image must be inverted, a same side image upright.

examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer builds the diagram from the two construction rays rather than sketching where it thinks the image goes, and then reads the image's nature off the drawing instead of recalling it. It knows that a real image needs converging rays, which is why it can explain both the magnifying glass and the concave lens from a single idea rather than two rules. It draws virtual rays dashed because it understands that the light is not there. And it checks the finished diagram against the far-side-means-inverted rule before moving on.
